summary:
Mark a sample, release it, catch a second sample and count how many are marked: the share of marked animals in the second sample estimates the share of the whole population. It returns population estimate (Lincoln–Petersen), chapman-corrected estimate, standard error and 95% lower bound, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator gives the Lincoln–Petersen estimate, the Chapman small-sample correction and a confidence interval. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mark–Recapture Population (Lincoln–Petersen)
sections.html:
N ≈ (M × C) ÷ R, with Chapman's correction N = [(M+1)(C+1) ÷ (R+1)] − 1

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Mmarked and released in the first sampleindividuals
Ctotal caught in the second sampleindividuals
Rmarked individuals in the second sampleindividuals
Nestimated population sizeindividuals

sections.title: How do I use the Mark–Recapture Population (Lincoln–Petersen)?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: animals marked and released (m) of 120 individuals, animals in the second sample (c) of 100 individuals, marked animals recaptured (r) of 22 individuals.

Substituting them into the formula gives population estimate (lincoln–petersen) of 545.45 individuals, chapman-corrected estimate of 530.35 individuals, standard error of 527.58 individuals, 95% lower bound of -3,389.75 individuals, 95% upper bound of 4,450.44 individuals.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
R above 20Reliablethe estimate is stable and the interval is narrow
R 5 – 20Use the correctionChapman's version removes most of the bias
R below 5Poorcollect another sample; the interval is wider than the estimate

  • The method assumes a closed population (no births, deaths, immigration or emigration between samples), equal catchability and that marks are not lost.

  • Trapshy animals violate equal catchability and inflate the estimate; baited traps and trap-happy animals deflate it.

  • The Chapman estimator is less biased than the plain ratio at the sample sizes field biologists actually achieve.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Sampling too soon after marking, before the animals have mixed back into the population.
  • Marking only the largest individuals, which makes them easier to recapture.
  • Reporting a point estimate with no interval, which overstates what a single sample can say.

faq.q: Why is my recapture rate so low?
faq.a: Either the population is large or the second sample was small; the estimator needs at least five to twenty recaptures to be meaningful.

faq.q: What if marked animals die from handling?
faq.a: That violates the closure assumption and biases the estimate; use a model that allows for losses on capture (Cormack–Jolly–Seber).

faq.q: What does the Mark–Recapture Population (Lincoln–Petersen) actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns population estimate (Lincoln–Petersen), chapman-corrected estimate, standard error and 95% lower bound. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
